title: Enoch Walked with God, and God Took Him — Life, Death, Walking Together
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. What we are going to read today is the kind of passage most people would most like to skip when they read the Bible: a whole chapter of names and ages. So-and-so lived so many years, became the father of so-and-so, lived so many more years, then he died. And then the next man — the same sentence pattern, all over again.

I want to ask you not to skip it. Because there is a sound in this chapter that you will only hear if you read slowly — one sentence repeated eight times: "then he died." Like a bell, one stroke after another.

In the garden God had said, "in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die," and a great many people assume that sentence was never carried out, because Adam did not fall down dead that day. Chapter 5 is the ledger of that sentence. And then, just before the eighth stroke of the bell falls, one name is suddenly different.

Verse 1: "This is the book of the generations of Adam." In Hebrew that is סֵפֶר תּוֹלְדֹת (*sefer toledot*), "the book of the generations." The whole of Genesis is divided into eleven sections by that word "generations", *toledot* — and this is the only place where the word "book" has been set in front of it. The author is telling you something: what follows is a formal document, an official record.

Then, from verse 6 onwards, the same sentence pattern simply keeps repeating: "So-and-so lived so many years, then became the father of so-and-so. So-and-so lived after he became the father of so-and-so so many years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. All the days of so-and-so were so many years, then he died."

Brothers and sisters, that way of writing is not the author running out of words. It is the laying down of a rhythm, the way a piece of music holds a fixed line in the bass. The first time through you feel nothing. By the third time it strikes you as a little monotonous. And by the eighth — "then he died", וַיָּמֹת (*vayamot*) — the cold runs down your spine.

And notice that every single generation carries the same clause: "and became the father of other sons and daughters." A genealogy records one line only, but beside every generation there stood a great many other people. God's plan travels along one line — and he has not forgotten the names standing beside the line.

There is one more detail, and it is enormously important, in verse 3: "Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth." Now set that sentence beside chapter 1 verse 26. Chapter 1 verse 26 says that man was made "in our image, after our likeness" — God's image. Chapter 5 verse 3 says Seth was fathered in Adam's likeness, after Adam's image. The same pair of Hebrew words, בִּדְמוּתוֹ כְּצַלְמוֹ (*bidmuto ketsalmo*), with the source changed.

Brothers and sisters, that one sentence tells us two things at once. The bad news is that the image is now handed down through a fallen man, so every generation carries the crack. The good news is that it was not cut off. God's image is damaged; it has not been cancelled. In chapter 9 verse 6 God still says, "for God made man in his own image" — and he says it after the flood.
Those men in chapter 5 lived eight and nine hundred years. Are we meant to read those numbers literally?

Interpreters read them in several ways. One reads them literally, holding that conditions in the world before the flood were different. One holds that the figures carry the symbolic usage found in other ancient Near Eastern documents. One holds that the names stand for family lines rather than individuals. The position of these notes is this: the weight of this chapter does not rest on the numbers, it rests on the rhythm. The text flags its own emphasis clearly enough — however long a man lived, the ending is the same sentence: "then he died." And the one man who is singled out for special treatment is precisely the one for whom the text declines to tell us how many years he lived before he died; it says only that "God took him." So we can say honestly that several of these readings have serious advocates, and then put our strength where the text puts its own emphasis. Do not stand in the pulpit and preach an uncertainty as though it were a certainty.
2. Eight Strokes of the Bell: Death Is Real

Brothers and sisters, I want to spend a little time on those three words, "then he died", because there is nothing Chinese culture likes talking about less. We are superstitious about the number four. We say a person has "passed on", has "gone", is "no longer with us". Even standing in a hospital room we will not let that word out of our mouths.
But the Bible has no squeamishness about it whatsoever. It writes "he died" eight times, squarely and plainly, inside a formal document.

And look at the man who lasted longest: Methuselah, nine hundred and sixty-nine years. The longest life in the history of the human race — and the ending the text gives him is still those same three words: "then he died."

So this chapter is saying something extremely important: time does not solve death. Live one more year, one more hundred years, one more nine hundred years — the outcome is identical. Which means that if a person's hope is built on "a little more time", that hope is hollow.

Brothers and sisters, this is very practical for us today. We pour enormous effort into extending time — diet and exercise, investments, health screenings, planning. All of that is good, and Scripture praises diligence. But this chapter wants you to see one thing clearly: the line you are lengthening ends in the same full stop. The real question is not "how much longer can I live?" It is "who am I walking this stretch of road with?"
And that is exactly the answer this chapter is about to give us.
"Then he died", repeated eight times — isn't that too heavy to read?

It is heavy, and that is precisely the effect the text is after. God had said, "you will surely die", and a good many people finish reading that and feel it was only a form of words; chapter 5 takes the same sentence and, by repeating it eight times, turns it into a drumbeat you can actually hear. Scripture is not comforting anybody here; it is first making a person face what is real — and that is healthy faith, not gloom. And it is precisely because the first eight are all the same that the one in verse 24 lands so loudly. So when you preach this chapter, do not rush to the comfort. Let the weight sit for a moment, and then bring people to the exception. Ecclesiastes says, "It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting" — that is exactly the lesson being taught here.
3. A Light from the Original: to Walk With Is a Reflexive Verb
At verses 21 to 24 the rhythm suddenly breaks.

"Enoch lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Methuselah. After Methuselah's birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and became the father of more sons and daughters. All the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years. Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him."
The first thing: nowhere in that whole passage does "then he died" appear. The full stop that falls eight times across the chapter does not fall here.
The second thing: the phrase "walked with God" appears twice. Once in verse 22, and then again in verse 24. The author wants you to be quite certain you have not misread it.

The word behind "walked with" is וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ (*vayithalech*). Its root means "to walk", but the form used here is the intensive reflexive, and it carries the sense of walking back and forth, of going to and fro in one another's company. Brothers and sisters, where did we last meet this word? Genesis 3:8: "They heard Yahweh God's voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day." The same verb, in the same stem.

Do you see the contrast? In chapter 3, God walks up and down in the garden and the human beings hide. In chapter 5, one man comes back to the place where God walks, and walks there with him for three hundred years.

And the preposition standing in front of "walked" is אֶת (*et*), which means "together with". Not trailing behind. Not following at a distance. Shoulder to shoulder. Amos 3:3 asks a very practical question: "Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?" If two people are going to walk together for three hundred years, one of them is going to have to fall in with the other's pace.

The third thing: "God took him", לָקַח (*laqach*). That same verb is used in 2 Kings 2, when Elijah is taken up into heaven. The text does not tell us where Enoch went, or how he went; it says only that God took him away. Hebrews 11:5 sums it up: "By faith Enoch was taken away, so that he wouldn't see death, and he was not found, because God translated him."
"Walking with God" sounds abstract. What does it actually look like?

The Hebrew uses the reflexive form (הִתְהַלֵּךְ), which carries the sense of walking back and forth; the picture is a stroll, not a march. So its heart is something continuous, something daily, company that goes both ways — not the occasional mountaintop experience. Micah 6:8 puts it most clearly of all: "to walk humbly with your God." And Enoch's walking was not a matter of hiding away in a cave — chapter 5 says plainly that "after Methuselah's birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and became the father of more sons and daughters." He walked with God while he was raising a family. So what it actually looks like is this: in the days you already have, one more person walking alongside you. When you have a decision, you ask him. When you are grieved, you tell him. When you finish something, you thank him.
Enoch's walking began only after he fathered a son at sixty-five. Does that mean a person has to go through something before he will draw near to God?

The text records the fact and gives us no cause, so let us not turn it into a formula. But the timing really is worth noticing: the birth of a child pushes a person right up against the edge of his own competence. A great many people first genuinely need God somewhere like that. The reminder for us cuts both ways. On one side, do not think lightly of the turning points of a life — having a child, changing jobs, falling ill, burying someone you love; any one of them may be a door God has set there. On the other side, do not wait for the turning point. Enoch may well have been close to God before he was sixty-five; it is simply that the text begins its record there. The real weight lies on the number that follows: three hundred years. Where you began is not the point. How long you kept walking is.
4. Three Practical Questions about Walking Together
Brothers and sisters, "walking with God" sounds lovely — but what does it actually look like? Let me put three very practical questions to the text.

First, when did the walking begin? The text is quite specific: "After Methuselah's birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years." Which is to say, it started after he became a father at sixty-five. Brothers and sisters, that is a fascinating detail. Becoming a father is often the first time a man truly registers his own limits — you are holding a small life entirely outside your control, and all at once you know you need God. So if you are only now beginning to walk seriously with God, you are not late. Enoch's three hundred years are counted from sixty-five.

Second, what did the walking consist of? The text says he walked for three hundred years and "became the father of more sons and daughters." Notice what the text does not say. It does not say he moved up a mountain, cut himself off from other people, or prayed ten hours a day. He walked with God in the middle of raising children. Brothers and sisters, walking with God is not swapping your life for a different one. It is having a different companion in the life you already have.

Third, how does a man who walks with God see the world? Jude 14 to 15 records something Enoch said: he preached that the Lord was coming with ten thousands of his holy ones to execute judgement on the ungodly. So Enoch was not a man floating about in the clouds with no quarrel with anyone. He saw very clearly, and he spoke very straight. A person who genuinely walks with God usually sees this world's troubles more sharply, not more vaguely.

And at the end of the chapter, this line is handed on to the next generation. Verse 29 says Lamech named his son Noah, saying, "This one will comfort us in our work and in the toil of our hands, caused by the ground which Yahweh has cursed." The word "comfort" is יְנַחֲמֵנוּ (*yenachamenu*) — and the text is playing a game with sound here, because "Noah" and "comfort" chime together without sharing a root. Brothers and sisters, at the end of a list saturated with death, a father holds a newborn and says: perhaps this one is the comfort.
"He was not found, for God took him" — does that mean people who believe do not have to die?

No. Every other man in this chapter died, including Enoch's own son Methuselah, the longest-lived man in the Bible. Enoch is the exception, not the rule; the one comparable exception in Scripture is Elijah. Hebrews 11:5 says, "By faith Enoch was taken away, so that he wouldn't see death", and yet the end of that same chapter says of these people, "These all died in faith." So the right way to read it is this: Enoch is a sign, set there to let us see in advance that death is not the last word; but the one who actually deals with death is the one who came later, died, and rose again. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed" — and that is the hope shared by everyone who believes.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is making the long lifespans the point of the sermon. Some men will spend an entire message explaining pre-flood conditions, the atmosphere, genetics, the decline in longevity. Those discussions may be had — but the point of this chapter is not why they lived so long, it is those eight repetitions of "then he died." Spend the hour arguing about ages and the congregation never hears the bell at all.

The second is using the genealogy to calculate the date of creation. Adding up the years to arrive at a precise date for the world's beginning became very popular from the seventeenth century onwards. But genealogies in the Bible are permitted to skip generations — Matthew 1:8 runs Joram straight on to Uzziah and leaves three kings out in between. And the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch differ from one another by more than a thousand years in these very figures. The text itself has not handed us one agreed piece of arithmetic.

The third is preaching Enoch as a man entirely without sin. The text says he walked with God; it does not say he was sinless. If you turn him into a model of moral spotlessness, the reaction in the room will be "then I can never do it", and people give up. The test is simple: when the congregation has heard you, do they want to start walking today, or do they conclude that it is out of reach anyway?

The fourth is using Enoch's being taken to argue for some timetable of the rapture. This chapter gives no timetable whatsoever. Any teaching that sets people counting days has drifted away from the purpose of the text. The point of Enoch is the walking, not the manner of his leaving.

The fifth is preaching Enoch and never preaching the other eight. The overwhelming bulk of this chapter belongs to the eight men who "then died." If you pick out only the one exception, the congregation will conclude that faith means becoming an exception. But the great majority of believers will have those same three words at the end of their lives. What this chapter offers them is not "you too can avoid dying." It is "you too can walk with him."
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese families take genealogies and the veneration of ancestors extremely seriously — is this chapter not doing exactly the same thing? Brothers and sisters, the form looks very similar; the substance is different. A Chinese clan genealogy looks backwards — remember where I came from, live so as not to disgrace the forefathers. The genealogy in Genesis looks forwards — where is God's promise going to travel along this line? Every name in this chapter is not a destination; it is a stretch of road. So you can say this to your elders: you care about roots, and the Bible agrees with you entirely, because the whole book keeps family records; it is only that the Bible keeps its family records in order to point to the one who would come out of that line. And as for the difference between venerating ancestors and remembering them, this is the most practical lesson a Chinese believer has to learn: we remember, we give thanks, we honour our parents — but there is only one whom we worship.

The second question: the elders in my family are getting old, they are frightened of talking about death and think it unlucky — what should I do? My advice is this: do not force the conversation, but do not run away alongside them either. The posture this chapter gives us is candour — Scripture writes "then he died" eight times without the smallest flinch. You can come in from another side. Instead of asking "are you afraid of dying?", ask "who are you most grateful to in your whole life, and what is hardest for you to put down?" Psalm 90:12 says, "So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom." Counting our days is not a way of manufacturing fear; it is for the sake of wisdom. And the best preparation is very often not a conversation at all — it is that you yourself live out a peace your elders can see. That peace carries more persuasive weight than any argument you could make.
The elders in my family are getting old. Should I talk with them about death? Isn't that unlucky?

What chapter 5 does is say death out loud — eight times. Scripture never shies away from this subject, because shying away will not delay death by a single day; it only means the things that needed saying are said too late. In practice my advice is: do not open with funeral arrangements. Start with his life — ask him to tell you a story from when he was young, and listen to him. A person whose story has been heard right to the end is a person whose heart opens. Then you can come in on something very concrete: arrangements for his health, what he wants to leave and to whom, the people he would like to see. If he plainly resists, stop there and come back to it after a while. And the one thing that matters most of all — where he stands with God — do not save it for the last moment, and do not use fear to get there; telling it out of your own experience is far more use than arguing it out of doctrine.
7. Living 321 Out — Walking Together Means Handing Over the Direction
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson and tie it back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Enoch walking with God is the earliest sample in the Old Testament of what being with God looks like. And the Lord Jesus said of himself, "the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing." There was not one step in his whole life where he decided for himself which way to go. That is my example, and it is very concrete: not settling the route first and then asking God to bless it, but first watching where he is going.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter gives the word "standard" a very practical shape. Enoch walked for three hundred years, and in those three hundred years he must have come to countless forks in the road. Walking together means precisely this: at every fork, you ask again. A standard is not something you hang on the wall. It is something you use while you are walking.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — walking together requires a voice that keeps speaking. Galatians 5:25 says, "If we live by the Spirit, let's also walk by the Spirit." The word behind "walk" there carries the sense of keeping step with a column on the march. Brothers and sisters, walking together has a cadence to it. It is not haphazard.

Let Jesus be King — walking together has one very hard precondition: the other person sets the route. When two people walk together, one of them is falling in with the other's stride. Letting Jesus be King means admitting that the direction is not mine to set, and neither is the speed. Have you noticed that the place where we most easily fall out with God is usually not the direction but the pace? We are willing to go there. We are simply not willing to go there slowly.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — look carefully at how the text puts it: "God took him", not "Enoch went up." Even in that closing action, the subject of the sentence is God. The brightest thing in Enoch's whole life was still something God did with his own hand.

Establish God's system — inside a list saturated with death, God still keeps that line generation after generation, all the way into Noah's hands. Brothers and sisters, God's system does not run on one or two heroes; it runs on generation after generation of people who are willing to walk. You may never in your life become an Enoch — but you can be the one on the list who passes the line along. And that, in fact, is what has been going on all the way through those eight repetitions of "then he died."

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We very easily preach walking with God as a matter of intensity — how many hours of devotion a day, how long you pray, how faithfully you turn up. But what this chapter gives us is length, not intensity: three hundred years. And they were walked out in the days of raising sons and daughters. So please do not measure a brother's or a sister's spiritual condition by intensity. A person who can only manage ten quiet minutes a day but has kept it up for thirty years looks far more like Enoch than a person who burned hot for three months.
Which comes first, walking with God or working for God? My serving keeps me very busy — does that count as walking with him?

Serving is not the same thing as walking, and that needs saying plainly. Enoch walked for three hundred years and the text records no great achievement of his; Jude mentions a prophecy he spoke, but chapter 5 records only that he "walked with God." And Martha in Luke 10 was extremely busy — what the Lord Jesus said was, "Mary has chosen the good part." This is not to say that the work does not matter. It is to say that the order cannot be inverted: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The practical test is very simple: if every piece of your serving were stopped for a month, would you and God still have anything to say to each other? If the answer is no, then the relationship has been kept alive by the work all along. Repair that stretch this week; the ministry will not collapse for it.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same List
Brothers and sisters, one and the same list, falling into four different hearts, is read four completely different ways.

The proud heart finishes and thinks: "I am going to be the Enoch." This heart turns walking with God into a competition and quiet time into a report card, and goes back to the small group to compare whose devotions ran longer. Brothers and sisters, notice that the text says Enoch walked for three hundred years and does not record one boasting word from him. The people who are actually walking usually say very little.

The fearful heart finishes and thinks: "I will never make it that far." Three hundred years is a terrifying number. To a heart like that I want to say: Enoch did not walk three hundred years all at once; he walked them one day at a time. And God has never asked you to guarantee in advance that you can finish. He only invites you to walk today's step. Philippians 1:6 says that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion — the responsibility for finishing rests with him.

The ashamed heart finishes and thinks: "Someone like me is not fit to have his name on a list like that." Brothers and sisters, look carefully at who is on this list: Lamech's forefathers; the father of the Noah who would one day lie drunk in his tent; a whole row of men who all died in the end. This is not a roll of saints. It is a crowd of ordinary people. And God left out not one single name.

The wounded heart finishes and thinks: "God took Enoch — what about the person I loved?" A heart like this may have buried someone dear only recently, and reading eight repetitions of "then he died" hurts a great deal. I want to say this to you very carefully: this chapter does not dodge death. It sets death down squarely on the page, because God knows you do not need a religion that pretends nothing has happened. And 1 Thessalonians 4:13 says that we do not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope — notice that Paul does not say do not grieve. What he says is: not "like those who have no hope." You are allowed to weep. And you are allowed to weep with hope.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, read this chapter slowly, all the way through, out loud. Every time you reach "then he died", stop for three seconds. And when you have finished, go back and read verse 24 again. You will know then why I asked you to read it that way.

Second, make yourself a "walking list". Write down five decisions you have to make this week, and beside each of them write one line: have I asked him about this one? Walking with God is not adding one more activity to the diary. It is asking one more question on the road you were already on.

Third, count your days. Take a sheet of paper, write down how old you are now, and then write down how you would like people to describe you when you are seventy. Then look at today's calendar — is there any relationship at all between those two pieces of paper?

Fourth, have one conversation with an older person. Ask them who they are most grateful to in their whole life, and what is hardest for them to put down. You do not have to talk about death; you only have to listen. And you will discover that this act by itself is already the passing on of a line.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences: there is a whole chapter of the Bible that is nothing but a list, and it writes the same words — "then he died" — eight times over, and even the man who reached nine hundred and sixty-nine gets exactly the same ending; so the Bible is very honest, and it never pretends that time can solve death; and yet there is one man on that list whose paragraph has no full stop, and the reason given is a single sentence — he spent his whole life walking with God.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer measure my life by the length of its time; I will look instead at who I am walking with.
I declare that I will walk with God in the days of raising children and going out to work and coming home again, and that I do not have to swap my life for a different one first.
I declare that the direction is not mine to set, and neither is the speed; I am willing to fall in with his steps.
I declare that I will hand this line on to the next generation, because God's system is walked out one generation at a time.
This week I am supposed to "say a few sentences to God every day", but I usually break the chain after two days. What do I do?

Start by lowering the standard to something you are certain you can do. Three hundred years is a very long road, and long roads can only be walked with small steps. Three things work well in practice. First, tie it to an action you are certain to perform every day — the first mouthful of water, getting into the car, shutting down the computer. Second, set a quantity so small that you would be embarrassed not to do it — three sentences, say. Third, when the chain breaks, do not make a fresh resolution; simply carry on from where you are, and do not try to make up the days you missed. People usually give up not because they cannot do the thing, but because after breaking once they decide they are the sort of person who cannot. There were certainly days in those three hundred years when Enoch walked badly. The point the text makes is that he kept walking.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, I want it to be the four words at the head of verse 24: "Enoch walked with God."

Picture that document to yourself. Page after page, all of it the same sentence pattern: he lived so many years, he became the father of so-and-so, then he died. Like a bell, one stroke after another, tolling heavily down.
And then you turn to a certain page, and the sentence simply breaks off. No "then he died." In its place, a very quiet line: "Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him."

Brothers and sisters, what moves us in that passage is not that he did not die. It is that he walked for three hundred years. How many mornings in those three hundred years did he not want to get up? How many times was he laughed at? How many of those years went by with nothing whatsoever happening? The text records not one of them. It records only one thing: he kept walking.

And Hebrews 11:5 adds a very important note: "For he has had testimony given to him that before his translation he had been well pleasing to God." Which is to say, God's pleasure was given before the taking up. He did not find out at the end of the road that God was pleased with him. He knew it the whole way along.

Brothers and sisters, you do not have to wait until your life is over to find out what God's disposition towards you is. Immanuel means "God with us", and that Immanuel has already come; his name is Jesus. Enoch walked with God for three hundred years; and in our own time God came in person and walked with us for thirty-three, and at the end of it died for us.

The focus is not on how long I can live, not on whether my name will be remembered, and not on how well I walked today. The focus is on Jesus — he is the one who came over to us, who walks with us, and who walked to the cross for us. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us: this week, not to ask to walk fast, but only to keep walking — and to keep walking with him. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.
1. ★★ Chapter 5 repeats "then he died" eight times, and then changes the wording when it comes to Enoch. Why does the text make us hear eight strokes of the bell first?

2. ★★★ The Hebrew behind "walked with God" is a reflexive form, and the picture is a stroll rather than a march. How does that picture differ from what you had previously imagined "drawing near to God" to be?
3. ★ Enoch walked for three hundred years while he was raising sons and daughters. What does that say about the question of whether the spiritual life has to leave ordinary life behind?
4. ★★ The one man this chapter remembers is not the one who lived longest but the one who walked closest. Which of our values is that contrast meant to correct?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (my serving is my walking), fearful (afraid of dying, afraid of running out of time), ashamed (I have broken the chain too many times to dare start again), wounded (someone once used "you are not close enough to God" to crush me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ When did your last settled practice of drawing near to God break off? What was happening in your life at the time?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "If today were my last day, the one thing I would most want to go and say is …"
9. ★★ This week, which action that you are certain to perform every day will you tie your "three sentences a day" to? Name the action and name the slot.

Leader's reminder: questions five, seven and eight will touch death and the sense of failure. If someone thinks of a relative who has died and weeps, stop the discussion and stay with him; do not rush to supply an answer. If anyone is currently facing serious illness or bereavement, follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find pastoral or professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to send you a single word every day this week, and send one back to him, as a sign between you. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a chapter of the Bible that writes "then he died" eight times in a row. Second, only one man in it is different, and of him the text says he "walked with God" for three hundred years. Third, so what I have learned is that the length of a life is not the point; how closely you walk is. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: whose story you are going to go and listen to this week, and which slot your three sentences a day will go in. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to teach us, in the most ordinary of days, to walk to and fro with him.
